title: Trustworthy Deep Learning
desc: The mathematics of making models you can trust — uncertainty, calibration, robustness, and domain shift.

watch.title: CS229 Lecture 6 — probability review (already seen in ML section)
watch.focus: Review: Bayes theorem. Now focus on: what it means to put a distribution over MODEL PARAMETERS — the shift from frequentist to Bayesian ML.

concept.title: Two ways to think about probability
concept.body:
Frequentist: probability = long-run frequency. Parameters are fixed, unknown. Bayesian: probability = degree of belief. Parameters have distributions. Update with Bayes: P(θ|data) ∝ P(data|θ)·P(θ).

For trustworthy DL: Bayesian thinking lets us say "the model is uncertain about its own parameters" — the foundation of epistemic uncertainty.
concept.analogy: Frequentist: 'this coin lands heads 50% of the time' — about the coin's physical property. Bayesian: 'I believe 50% chance this coin is biased' — about your state of knowledge before flipping.
concept.visual:
Bayes: P(θ|D) ∝ P(D|θ)·P(θ)
Posterior ∝ Likelihood × Prior
MLE = MAP with uniform prior
L2 reg = MAP with Gaussian prior
Bayesian DL: full posterior → approximate

challenge.q: You train a NN with MLE. From Bayesian perspective, what prior does MLE implicitly assume?

opts.t: Uniform prior — all parameter values equally likely before data
MLE has no connection to Bayesian inference

challenge.hint: MAP = argmax[log P(D|θ)+log P(θ)]. When P(θ) is constant, MAP = ?
challenge.exp: MLE implicitly assumes a uniform prior — all parameter settings equally plausible before data. L2 regularization adds a Gaussian prior. This connection means every training decision is a probabilistic choice.

project.title: Prior Sensitivity Experiment
project.desc: Train same model with different regularization strengths. Interpret each as a prior.
deliverables: Train 4 nets: no reg, L2(weak), L2(strong), L1
Measure test accuracy + ECE for each
Plot: regularization strength vs ECE
README: interpret each setting as a Bayesian prior. What is strong L2 saying about your beliefs?
project.hint: weight_decay in Adam controls L2. Plot weight histograms — does Gaussian prior → Gaussian weights?

units.title: Aleatoric vs Epistemic Uncertainty
units.meta: What kind of uncertainty is it?

watch.title: Kendall & Gal 2017 "What Uncertainties Do We Need?" — abstract + section 1
watch.focus: Foundational paper for uncertainty types in deep learning. Formal definitions of aleatoric and epistemic, how to decompose them in practice.

concept.title: Not all uncertainty is the same
concept.body:
Aleatoric: inherent randomness in data. Blurry image will always be uncertain — more data does not help. Epistemic: model ignorance. Reducible with more data. Captured by uncertainty over model parameters.

Total = aleatoric + epistemic. MC Dropout: epistemic ≈ Var[E(y|x,θ)], aleatoric ≈ E[Var(y|x,θ)].
concept.analogy: Aleatoric: measuring boiling liquid temperature — it fluctuates by nature. Epistemic: not knowing the boiling point of an unknown liquid — more experiments resolve this.
concept.visual:
Total uncertainty = Aleatoric + Epistemic
Aleatoric: E[Var(y|x,θ)] — avg predicted variance
Epistemic: Var[E(y|x,θ)] — variance of mean preds
MC Dropout approximates both simultaneously

challenge.q: Model uncertain on rare pediatric disease it has never seen. After 10,000 more images, uncertainty drops. Which type?

opts.t: Uncertainty should not change with data

challenge.hint: If uncertainty decreases with more data, what type is it by definition?
challenge.exp: Epistemic — reducible from lack of training data. Adding examples reduced model ignorance. If aleatoric (inherent image ambiguity), more data would not help.

project.title: Uncertainty Decomposition
project.desc: Train with MC Dropout on MNIST. Decompose into aleatoric and epistemic.
deliverables: Train CNN with dropout on MNIST
MC Dropout (T=50) on: MNIST test, rotated MNIST, Fashion-MNIST
Compute: total entropy, epistemic (variance of means), aleatoric (mean of variances)
Plot all three for each input type
README: what does each component tell you about model reliability?
project.hint: Epistemic = Var[mean softmax across T runs]. Aleatoric = mean[entropy of each softmax run].

watch.title: MacKay "Information Theory, Inference, Learning" — Chapter 1 (free PDF)
watch.focus: Entropy definition, KL divergence definition and asymmetry. 20 min read.

concept.title: Quantifying uncertainty with information theory
concept.body: Entropy H(p) = −Σp(x)log p(x): how spread out a distribution is. High entropy = high uncertainty. KL Divergence KL(p||q) = Σp(x)log(p(x)/q(x)): how different q is from reference p. Not symmetric. Used in variational inference as the regularization term.
concept.analogy: Entropy: shuffled deck = maximum uncertainty about next card. Sorted deck = zero entropy. KL: extra bits needed if you assume sorted (q) but it's actually shuffled (p).
concept.visual:
H(p) = -Σp(x)log₂p(x)  [bits]
Uniform over 4 classes: H=2 bits (maximum)
Certain (one class=1): H=0 bits

KL(p||q) ≥ 0, = 0 only when p=q
KL(p||q) ≠ KL(q||p)  (asymmetric!)

challenge.q: Model A: [0.97,0.01,0.01,0.01]. Model B: [0.25,0.25,0.25,0.25]. Which has higher entropy?

opts.t: Model A: higher entropy, less trustworthy
Model B: higher entropy — completely uncertain; Model A is highly confident

challenge.hint: Entropy is maximized by the uniform distribution.
challenge.exp: Model B has maximum entropy (H=2 bits) — completely uncertain. Model A has very low entropy — highly confident. For a calibrated model, high confidence (low entropy) should correlate with high accuracy. Entropy is your uncertainty score per prediction.

project.title: Entropy as a Trust Signal
project.desc: Use prediction entropy as an automatic abstention system.
deliverables: Train classifier, compute entropy of softmax for test set
Histogram: entropy for correct vs incorrect predictions
Set threshold: abstain if H > threshold
Plot accuracy vs coverage curve
README: what threshold gives the best tradeoff for your use case?
project.hint: Entropy = -sum(p*log(p+1e-8)). Plot x=coverage (% predictions made), y=accuracy of those predictions.

watch.title: Gal & Ghahramani 2016 "Dropout as Bayesian Approximation" — abstract + sections 1-2
watch.focus: Key insight: keeping dropout ON at test time approximates sampling from the posterior over weights.

concept.title: Dropout at test time = approximate Bayesian inference
concept.body:
Standard dropout: random neuron zeroing during training only. MC Dropout: keep it ON at test time. Run T passes — each samples a different subnetwork, approximating P(θ|data).

Mean of T predictions = final answer. Variance = epistemic uncertainty. No retraining needed.
concept.analogy: Ask 50 doctors who each randomly ignore some knowledge. Average diagnoses → reliable. Disagreement → your uncertainty.
concept.visual:
T forward passes with dropout ON
predictions = [f(x,θ₁),...,f(x,θ_T)]
mean = Σ preds/T  ← final prediction
variance = Var(preds) ← epistemic uncertainty
T=50 is usually sufficient

challenge.q: MC Dropout (T=100): 95 runs say "normal", 5 say "pneumonia". Variance is high. What should system do?

opts.t: Report "normal" with HIGH uncertainty flag for clinical review
Reject image, request a new one

challenge.hint: The variance IS the uncertainty signal. In safety-critical systems, what do you do with high-variance predictions?
challenge.exp: Report "normal" with HIGH uncertainty flag. The 5 dissenting runs represent real model uncertainty. A trustworthy system surfaces this to the clinician. The clinician makes the final call on ambiguous cases.

project.title: MC Dropout Spatial Uncertainty Map
project.desc: Add MC Dropout to medical image classifier. Visualize WHERE the model is uncertain spatially.
deliverables: Add dropout layers to classifier
T=50 MC Dropout inference passes per image
Spatial uncertainty: variance per region → uncertainty heatmap
Overlay heatmap on original image
Compare: does uncertainty highlight clinically ambiguous regions?
project.hint: Variance per region: run T passes with activation hooks, compute variance across passes.

watch.title: Lakshminarayanan et al. 2017 — abstract + section 3
watch.focus: Why ensembles work (diversity in function space), how to train them, why they outperform MC Dropout on calibration.

concept.title: Automated second opinions
concept.body: Train N independent models (different seeds). Average predictions at inference. Variance across models = uncertainty. Each model finds a different local minimum — together they explore more of the posterior. Simple, strong, expensive.
concept.analogy: You wouldn't trust one doctor for a difficult diagnosis. Get second and third opinions. Deep ensembles are automated second opinions. Their disagreement is honest uncertainty.
concept.visual:
N=5 independent training runs
Model i: p_i(y|x)
Mean: p̄ = (1/N)·Σ p_i
Variance: Var[p_i] ← uncertainty
Higher N → better but more expensive

challenge.q: MC Dropout (T=50) vs Deep Ensembles (N=5) on a resource-constrained robot. Which do you choose?

opts.t: Ensembles — always better regardless of resources
MC Dropout — acceptable uncertainty at 5× lower compute cost

challenge.hint: Ensembles require 5× memory and inference time. MC Dropout uses one model with T passes.
challenge.exp: MC Dropout is the practical choice. N=5 ensembles require 5× memory and inference time. MC Dropout: one model, tune T based on available compute. Quality difference exists but is acceptable for many robotics applications.

project.title: Ensemble vs MC Dropout Comparison
project.desc: Train ensemble of 5 models. Compare against MC Dropout.
deliverables: Train 5 independent models (different seeds) for ensemble
Add MC Dropout to single model, T=50 passes
Compare: ECE, AUROC (OOD detection), inference time per image
Calibration curves for both methods
README: when would you choose each? Be specific about deployment context.
project.hint: Same architecture for all. ECE and AUROC are your main metrics. time.perf_counter() for latency.

watch.title: Angelopoulos & Bates 2021 "A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction" — sections 1-3
watch.focus: Coverage guarantee, nonconformity scores, how to compute q̂. Clearest introduction to conformal prediction.

concept.title: Prediction sets with statistical guarantees
concept.body:
Output a set of classes guaranteed to contain the true label with probability ≥ 1−α. How: compute nonconformity scores on calibration set. Find q̂ = (1−α) quantile. At test: include all classes with score ≤ q̂.

Key guarantee: P(Y ∈ Ĉ(X)) ≥ 1−α regardless of distribution. Finite-sample, distribution-free. Rare and powerful.
concept.analogy: Instead of 'this is pneumonia (90% confident)', say 'diagnosis is in {pneumonia, pleural effusion} — guaranteed to contain the true diagnosis 90% of the time.' Smaller set = more informative = better model.

challenge.q: α=0.10, predictor outputs singletons for 60% of images, size 2+ for 40%. What does set size tell you?

opts.t: Large sets mean model is wrong — should always output singletons
Large sets reflect genuine ambiguity — the model is honest about hard cases
Set size is unrelated to confidence

challenge.hint: The guarantee holds regardless of set size. What does a larger set communicate about that specific input?
challenge.exp: Large sets reflect genuine ambiguity — the model cannot confidently distinguish the included classes. Honest and useful. Smaller average set size while maintaining coverage = better discrimination = better model.

project.title: Conformal Classifier for Medical Imaging
project.desc: Build conformal predictor. Analyze sets. Verify coverage.
deliverables: Split: training, calibration (fresh), test sets
Compute nonconformity scores, find q̂ for α=0.05, 0.10, 0.20

README: how would you present conformal sets to a radiologist?
project.hint: Nonconformity score = 1-softmax[true_class]. np.quantile(scores, 1-alpha) gives q̂. Compute q̂ on CALIBRATION set only.

watch.title: Guo et al. 2017 "On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks" — abstract + sections 1-3
watch.focus: What ECE measures, the reliability diagram, why modern deep nets are overconfident.

concept.title: When 90% confident means 90% accurate
concept.body: A model is calibrated if stated confidence matches actual accuracy. Most deep networks are overconfident. ECE: bin predictions by confidence, measure |accuracy − confidence| per bin, weight by bin size. ECE=0 is perfect. ECE>0.05 concerning for safety-critical use.
concept.analogy: Weather forecaster saying '70% rain' should be right 70% of those days. Says 70%, rains 40% — overconfident. ECE measures this gap systematically.
concept.visual:
Reliability diagram:
x=confidence bins, y=accuracy
Perfect: on diagonal y=x
Overconfident: points below diagonal
ECE = Σ(|B|/n)·|acc(B)-conf(B)|

challenge.q: 100 predictions, confidence 0.80–0.90, 65 correct. Calibration error for this bin?
challenge.exp: |0.85-0.65| = 0.20. Model claims 85% but is right 65% — 20pp overconfident. For medical AI, 0.20 ECE in the high-confidence range is dangerous.

project.title: Calibration Audit Pipeline
project.desc: Build a reusable calibration audit tool.
deliverables: Compute ECE with configurable bins (10, 15, 20)
Plot reliability diagram with per-bin confidence intervals

project.hint: reliability_from_predictions(y_true, y_prob, n_bins) → ECE, bin_accs, bin_confs. Make it reusable across all experiments.

units.title: Temperature Scaling
units.meta: One parameter to calibrate any model

watch.title: Guo et al. 2017 — section 4: Temperature Scaling
watch.focus: How temperature scaling works, why it doesn't change accuracy, how to tune T.

concept.title: Post-hoc calibration without retraining
concept.body: Divide logits by T>1 before softmax. T>1 = softer (less confident). T<1 = sharper. Tune T on validation set by minimizing NLL. No retraining. Accuracy unchanged because argmax(logits/T) = argmax(logits).
concept.analogy: Volume dial on a speaker. Music (predictions) stays the same — you adjust how loud (confident) it sounds. Turn down (T>1) → sounds less certain, usually more accurately.
concept.visual:
calibrated_logits = logits/T
T>1: softer softmax, lower confidence
T<1: sharper, higher confidence
Tune: minimize NLL(val, logits/T) over T∈[0.1,10]
accuracy unchanged: argmax(L/T) = argmax(L)

challenge.q: After temperature scaling T=2.5: ECE drops 0.12→0.03, accuracy stays identical. Why?

opts.t: Temperature scaling changes probabilities but not the argmax prediction
T=2.5 too small to affect model

challenge.hint: Does dividing all logits by T change which class has the highest logit?
challenge.exp: argmax(logits/T) = argmax(logits) — relative ordering unchanged. Predicted class never changes → accuracy identical. Only probabilities change (softer) → fixes overconfidence.

watch.title: Goodfellow et al. 2015 "Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples" — abstract + sections 1-3
watch.focus: What FGSM is, the sign(gradient) intuition, why adversarial examples exist.

concept.title: Inputs designed to fool your model
concept.body:
FGSM: x_adv = x + ε·sign(∇_x L). One step increasing loss. Fast but weak. PGD: iterative FGSM with projection back to ε-ball. Stronger attack, standard benchmark.

For physical systems: adversarial patches can fool detection in the real world.
concept.analogy: A forged painting looks identical to humans but has subtle patterns fooling an AI authentication system. FGSM finds the minimal change that maximally confuses the classifier.
concept.visual:
FGSM: x_adv = x + ε·sign(∇_x L)
PGD: repeat T times:
  x = x + α·sign(∇_x L)
  x = clip(x, x_orig-ε, x_orig+ε)
ε = max perturbation budget (e.g. 8/255)

challenge.q: FGSM uses sign(∇_x L) — the sign, not the full gradient. Why?

opts.t: Sign ensures equal ε perturbation per pixel under L∞ constraint — maximally effective within the budget

challenge.hint: FGSM operates under L∞ norm ball of radius ε. What does sign() do to each pixel?
challenge.exp: L∞: every pixel can change by at most ε. sign(gradient) gives ±ε per pixel — maximally effective under this constraint. Raw gradient would give larger changes to high-gradient pixels — less efficient under L∞ budget.

project.title: Adversarial Attack & Defense

project.hint: x_adv = (x + eps*x.grad.sign()).clamp(0,1). model.zero_grad(), loss.backward() for gradients.

watch.title: Quinonero-Candela "Dataset Shift in Machine Learning" — chapter 1
watch.focus: Covariate shift definition, label shift, why standard ML assumes i.i.d. data and why this fails in deployment.

concept.title: The deployment gap — the real trustworthiness problem
concept.body: Covariate shift: P(X) changes, P(Y|X) same. Scanner differences in medical imaging. Domain generalization: train on multiple sources, deploy on unseen target. Techniques: data augmentation, domain adversarial training, test-time adaptation.
concept.analogy: Training a driver in sunny California, deploying in Norwegian winter. Driving rules are the same. Visual inputs are completely different — snow, ice, darkness.
concept.visual:
Source: Hospital A, B, C
Target: Hospital D (unseen)
Goal: model on A+B+C → generalizes to D
Covariate shift: P(X_A) ≠ P(X_D), P(Y|X) same

challenge.q: Model: 91% on Hospital A, 68% on Hospital B (same disease). First thing you measure?

opts.t: Retrain on Hospital B data immediately
Measure calibration and uncertainty at B — is the model at least uncertain about its errors?

challenge.hint: Before fixing, diagnose. Confidently wrong vs appropriately uncertain — completely different responses.
challenge.exp: Diagnose first. Confidently wrong at B = dangerous calibration + shift problem. Uncertain on B errors = coverage problem, fixable with targeted data. The uncertainty signal tells you whether the model knows it's failing.
